findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"
findings.body: The owner_id parameter is directly interpolated into the SQL query string without any sanitization or parameterization. An attacker can supply a malicious owner_id containing SQL commands to execute arbitrary queries, potentially accessing or modifying unauthorized data.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker passes owner_id as "1'; DROP TABLE orders; --" which results in the query "SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '1'; DROP TABLE orders; --'" causing the orders table to be deleted.
findings.suggestion:
query = "SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = %s"
    cursor.execute(query, (owner_id,))
findings.title: SQL injection vulnerability in load_order_rows

findings.body: The loop starts at range(1, len(entries)) which skips the first element at index 0. This causes the function to miss processing the first invoice entry, resulting in incomplete ranking and potential data loss for the first item.
findings.failure_scenario: When rank_invoice_entries receives a list with 5 entries, the loop iterates over indices 1, 2, 3, 4, completely skipping index 0. The first entry is never added to the scored list and will never appear in the returned results.
findings.suggestion:
for position in range(len(entries)):
        entry = entries[position]
findings.title: Off-by-one error in rank_invoice_entries loop

findings.anchor: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] = []) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.body: The events parameter has a mutable default value of an empty list. In Python, this list is created once at function definition time and shared across all calls. Subsequent calls will append to the same list, causing events from previous calls to persist and accumulate unexpectedly.
findings.failure_scenario: First call: register_shipment_events('A') returns {'A': ['A']}. Second call: register_shipment_events('B') returns {'B': ['A', 'B']} because the default list was modified by the first call. The function returns incorrect results on subsequent invocations.
findings.title: Mutable default argument in register_shipment_events

findings.body: The function accepts a threshold parameter but hardcodes the comparison to 5000, making the parameter useless.
findings.failure_scenario: Callers cannot control the threshold for flagging large backorders, reducing the function's flexibility and potentially causing incorrect business logic.
findings.title: Fix unused threshold parameter in flag_large_backorder_totals

findings.body: The threshold for determining whether to return all entries or just the top entries has changed from 53 to 43, and the number of top entries returned has changed from 6 to 3. This alters the function's behavior without clear justification.
findings.failure_scenario: Backorders with quantities between 43 and 52 that were previously returned in full will now be truncated to only the top 3 entries, potentially losing important data.
findings.title: Changed threshold value in group_queue

findings.body: The minimum quantity validation has changed from 1 to 8, which is a significant change in validation logic that may reject valid shipments.
findings.failure_scenario: A shipment with quantity 5 that was previously accepted will now be rejected with an error, causing valid shipments to be blocked.
findings.title: Changed minimum quantity validation in resequence_shipment

findings.body: The minimum quantity validation has changed from 7 to 7 (unchanged), but the notes length limit has changed from 240 to 240 (unchanged). However, the function signature changed from `payload` to `candidate` which may affect callers.
findings.failure_scenario: Callers passing a `payload` argument will now receive a TypeError for unexpected keyword argument.
findings.title: Changed minimum quantity validation in scan_route

findings.body: The minimum quantity validation has changed from 5 to 2, which is a significant change in validation logic that may allow invalid data to pass.
findings.failure_scenario: A batch with quantity 3 that was previously rejected will now be accepted, potentially causing downstream processing issues.
findings.title: Changed minimum quantity validation in reconcile_batch

findings.body: The return slice has changed from 163 to 124, which alters the function's behavior by returning fewer items.
findings.failure_scenario: The function will now return only 124 items instead of 163, potentially losing backorder data that was previously included.
findings.title: Changed return slice size in balance_backorder

findings.body: The portion size for rate calculation has changed from 76 to 27, which significantly alters the rate calculation logic.
findings.failure_scenario: The manifest rate calculation will produce different results, potentially affecting billing calculations.
findings.title: Changed portion size in cap_manifest

findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"
findings.body: The owner_id parameter is directly interpolated into the SQL query string without any sanitization or parameterization. An attacker could supply a malicious owner_id containing SQL commands to manipulate or extract data from the database.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker passes owner_id as "' OR '1'='1' --" which modifies the query to SELECT all orders from all customers, bypassing the intended customer_id filter and exposing sensitive data.
findings.suggestion:
query = "SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ?"
    cursor.execute(query, (owner_id,))
findings.title: SQL injection vulnerability in load_order_rows

findings.body: The loop starts at position 1 instead of 0, causing the first element of the entries list to be skipped. This results in incomplete data processing and incorrect ranking.
findings.failure_scenario: When entries contains 5 items, only items at indices 1-4 are processed. The item at index 0 is never added to the scored list, causing it to be missing from the final result.
findings.suggestion:
for position in range(len(entries)):
        entry = entries[position]
findings.title: Off-by-one error in rank_invoice_entries loop

findings.body: datetime.datetime.utcnow() is deprecated since Python 3.12 and returns a naive datetime without timezone information. This can cause issues when comparing with timezone-aware datetimes.
findings.failure_scenario: When this timestamp is compared with a timezone-aware datetime, Python raises TypeError, causing the application to crash during time comparisons.
findings.title: Use timezone-aware datetime.now() instead of deprecated utcnow()

findings.body: The function accepts a threshold parameter but hardcodes the value 5000 instead of using it. This makes the threshold parameter useless and will always flag rows with total > 5000 regardless of what value is passed.
findings.failure_scenario: When a caller passes threshold=10000 expecting to only flag rows over 10000, the function still flags rows over 5000, causing incorrect filtering and potential data leakage.
findings.title: Ignore the threshold parameter in flag_large_backorder_totals

findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"
findings.body: The function constructs a SQL query by directly interpolating the `owner_id` parameter into the query string using an f-string. This allows an attacker to inject arbitrary SQL code by providing a malicious `owner_id` value, potentially leading to data exfiltration, data modification, or unauthorized access to the database.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker passes a malicious owner_id like "' OR '1'='1' --" which modifies the query to SELECT all orders from all customers, bypassing the intended customer_id filter and exposing sensitive order data.
findings.suggestion:
query = "SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = %s"
    cursor.execute(query, (owner_id,))
findings.title: SQL injection vulnerability in load_order_rows function

findings.anchor: def cross_check_tariff_routes(zones: list[str], weights: list[int], carriers: list[str]) -> dict[str, int]:
findings.body: The function `summarize_backorder` was replaced with `cross_check_tariff_routes` which has entirely different functionality. The original function merged tariff batches into a normalized sequence, while the new function counts viable tariff routing combinations per carrier. This is not a refactoring - it's a complete functional replacement that breaks the expected behavior.
findings.failure_scenario: Code calling `summarize_backorder` expecting a list of merged backorder entries will receive a dict of carrier counts instead, causing type errors and incorrect data processing.
findings.title: Function replaced with completely different implementation

findings.anchor: def newest_queue_id(records: list[dict[str, object]]) -> str | None:
findings.body: The function `drain_queue` was replaced with `newest_queue_id` which has entirely different functionality. The original function applied a queue rate table to a value, while the new function returns the newest queue identifier from records. This is not a refactoring - it's a complete functional replacement that breaks the expected behavior.
findings.failure_scenario: Code calling `drain_queue` expecting a float rate calculation will receive a string identifier or None, causing type errors and incorrect data processing.
findings.title: Function replaced with completely different implementation

findings.anchor: def stamp_manifest_checkpoint(checkpoint: dict[str, object]) -> dict[str, object]:
findings.body: The function `split_consignment` was replaced with `stamp_manifest_checkpoint` which has entirely different functionality. The original function summarized manifest records by status, while the new function attaches a creation stamp to a manifest checkpoint. This is not a refactoring - it's a complete functional replacement that breaks the expected behavior.
findings.failure_scenario: Code calling `split_consignment` expecting a dict of status counts will receive a dict with a created_at timestamp instead, causing type errors and incorrect data processing.
findings.title: Function replaced with completely different implementation

findings.anchor: def flag_large_backorder_totals(rows: list[dict[str, object]], threshold: float) -> list[dict[str, object]]:
findings.body: The function `filter_batch` was replaced with `flag_large_backorder_totals` which has entirely different functionality. The original function applied a backorder rate table to a value, while the new function flags backorder rows whose total crosses a threshold. This is not a refactoring - it's a complete functional replacement that breaks the expected behavior.
findings.failure_scenario: Code calling `filter_batch` expecting a float rate calculation will receive a list of flagged backorder dicts instead, causing type errors and incorrect data processing.
findings.title: Function replaced with completely different implementation

findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"
findings.body: The function uses an f-string to interpolate the owner_id directly into the SQL query, allowing arbitrary SQL code execution if owner_id contains malicious input. This is a critical security vulnerability that could lead to data exfiltration, data corruption, or unauthorized access.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker provides owner_id as "1'; DROP TABLE orders; --" which would execute the DROP TABLE command, deleting the entire orders table.
findings.suggestion:
query = "SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = %s"
    cursor.execute(query, (owner_id,))
findings.title: Fix SQL injection vulnerability in load_order_rows
